title: A wheezy 3-year-old after a cold
desc: This station involves a focused history from the mother of a 3-year-old boy brought to a metropolitan ED with wheeze and breathlessness that came on overnight after 2 days of a cold, then a focused examination. The candidate interprets his observations and a respiratory viral PCR, assesses severity, diagnoses viral-induced (preschool) wheeze, and outlines ED management, spacer teaching and safety netting.
focus: Acute wheeze in a preschool child: a BINDS-based paediatric history, excluding anaphylaxis and an inhaled foreign body, grading severity, and managing viral-induced wheeze with spacer teaching
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. It is early morning. Wesley Morgan, a 3-year-old boy, has been brought in by his parents because they are worried about his breathing. Last night he became more and more wheezy, and now he is short of breath. He is in a paediatric acute bay, sitting on his mother's lap with a saturation probe on. His mother, Kate, will answer your questions. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations, weighed him and taken a nose swab.
tasks: Take a focused history from Wesley's mother and perform a focused examination of Wesley, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Wesley's observations and his respiratory viral PCR result. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Kate Morgan, Wesley's mother. Wesley is 3 years old. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are worried and tired after a night with no sleep, but calm enough to give a clear history. Wesley's dad, Ben, came in with you and is getting a coffee. Wesley is imagined (or a doll) on your lap. He is grizzly, clingy and breathing fast. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Wesley came in with Mum and Dad about 25 minutes ago. At triage at 06:40 he was resp rate 44, sats 94% on room air, heart rate 155, BP 98/62, temperature 37.8, cap refill 2 seconds, with moderate work of breathing. Repeat at 06:55: resp rate 46, sats 93%, heart rate 158. He weighs 15 kg. I've taken a nose swab for the respiratory virus PCR. Mum gave him two puffs of his sister's salbutamol at home at about 5 o'clock. What would you like?"

How Wesley changes with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for salbutamol, the nurse asks, "How many puffs, and how would you like it given?" If they say 6 puffs of salbutamol by puffer and spacer with a mask, the nurse gives it. The examiner then says, "20 minutes later: resp rate 40, sats 95%, heart rate 156. He has less recession, but there is still mild subcostal recession and a wheeze. He is a little more settled. His heart rate is still fast because of the salbutamol; he is otherwise improving."
  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "His sats are 93%. What target are you aiming for?" Credit a candidate who says oxygen is not needed unless sats fall below 92%.
  • If they keep Wesley calm on your lap and explain things to you, you settle a little.
  • If they do nothing for his breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says, "He's working harder now. Resp rate 50, sats 91%, and he's getting quite upset."
  • If they ask for the senior doctor, the nurse says, "The paeds registrar is in resus. They'll come as soon as they can. Keep going."
  • If they ask for an X-ray, bloods or the swab result, the examiner says any results will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I'm worried about Wesley. He's had a cold for the past two days, but now he's getting worse."

History (give only when asked):

The breathing

  • The noise: it is a whistling sound when he breathes out. "It sounds like his older sister's asthma."
  • Stridor: if the candidate describes or imitates a harsh noise on breathing in: "No, it hasn't sounded like that."
  • Onset: "We only noticed it getting bad overnight. It came on within a few hours." It has been bad like this for about 3 hours. It is constant and getting worse.
  • What helps: "We tried giving him a couple of puffs of his sister's puffer (salbutamol) and that might have helped a little." You gave it at about 5 am, straight into his mouth. You do not have a spacer.
  • What makes it worse: nothing that you have noticed.
  • The cold: runny nose and a bit of a cough for 2 days. "His cold has got better, but it's his breathing that's worse now." He felt a bit warm last night, but you did not take his temperature.
  • How he is: more tired than normal and "not himself". He is talking in short bits because he is puffed. His lips have not gone blue.
  • Eating, drinking and wees: he is eating less and seems too tired to eat. He is drinking a little. He is passing less urine than usual.
  • Before: he had bronchiolitis at 8 months. "Could this be that again?" He was seen at hospital then and did not need intensive care or help with his breathing. He has had no wheezy episodes since. He does not cough or wheeze at night, or when running or laughing, when he is well.

Triggers (only if asked)

  • He goes to day-care and "catches everything". Several children there have had colds.
  • Smoking: "I still smoke, about 10 a day. I try to keep it outside, but sometimes it's too cold or wet." Ben does not smoke.

Things the candidate may ask to rule out (all no unless stated)

  • Allergic reaction: no rash or hives, no swelling of the lips, face or tongue, no vomiting, no floppiness. No new foods, no bites or stings. Never had a serious allergic reaction.
  • Something inhaled: no sudden choking or coughing fit. "His sister has Lego, but I've never seen him choke on anything."
  • Croup or epiglottitis: no barking cough, no hoarse or muffled voice, no drooling, not leaning forward to breathe.
  • Whooping cough: no coughing fits, no whoop, no vomiting after coughing.
  • Long-term chest problems: his newborn heel-prick test was normal. No long-lasting wet cough. He is growing well. His poos are normal.
  • Floppy airway: he has never had noisy breathing when he is well.

Background (BINDS)

  • Birth: born at 36 weeks and 4 days by normal vaginal delivery. No problems in the pregnancy.
  • Immunisations: up to date.
  • Nutrition: eats a varied diet but is fussy with vegetables. Eating less now.
  • Development: met all his milestones, with no loss of skills. "The nurse at his check said he's on the 65th centile for height and weight."
  • Sleep: poor sleep for the past 2 nights. He has been sleeping in your bed.
  • Toileting: toilet trained in the day, in nappies at night. Fewer wees than usual.

Past medical history: eczema since 6 months of age. Bronchiolitis at 8 months.

Medications: moisturiser and a steroid cream from the GP for his eczema (you cannot remember its name). The two puffs of his sister's salbutamol this morning. Nothing else.

Allergies: no food or medicine allergies.

Family history: his older sister Mia, aged 7, has asthma. Ben has eczema.

Social history

  • You and Ben are separated. Wesley and Mia live a week with each parent. This week they are with you.
  • Day-care Monday to Wednesday.
  • Your smoking is as above.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you wonder whether this is asthma like Mia's, or the bronchiolitis again. You are worried his breathing is getting worse and want something to help him now. You would like to know whether he will have to stay in hospital. You feel a bit guilty about the smoking but will only say so if it comes up.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is this going to turn into asthma like his sister's?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: alert, a bit grizzly but settles on his mother's lap; talking in short sentences, a little less than usual for him. Sitting upright. Pink, not cyanosed. Clear nasal discharge. No drooling. No stridor. Normal voice. Well grown (15 kg).
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported (or as above after salbutamol).
  • Work of breathing: RR 46. Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no tracheal tug, no nasal flaring, some abdominal breathing. No head bobbing, no grunting.
  • Chest: looks slightly hyperexpanded. Trachea central. Expansion equal. Resonant on percussion throughout. Widespread high-pitched expiratory wheeze on both sides with a prolonged expiratory phase. Air entry good and equal on both sides; not a silent chest. No focal crackles, no bronchial breathing.
  • Cardiovascular: HR 158, regular. Warm peripheries, central CRT 2 seconds. Heart sounds normal, no murmur.
  • Hydration: lips slightly dry, moist tongue, eyes not sunken, normal skin turgor. Not clinically dehydrated.
  • Skin: dry, slightly rough eczema patches in both elbow and knee creases. No urticaria, no angioedema, no petechiae.
  • ENT: mildly red throat, tonsils not enlarged, no exudate. Ear drums normal. A few small, soft, non-tender cervical lymph nodes.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Wesley's identity and Kate's relationship to him, and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises the increased work of breathing from the nurse's observations and acts before finishing the history: keeps Wesley calm on his mother's lap and asks for salbutamol 6 puffs by puffer and spacer with a mask.
check.d: Credit when salbutamol by spacer is requested within the first few minutes. No credit for nebulised salbutamol without a reason.

check.x: Communicates with the parent in plain words, acknowledges her worry, does not judge the smoking or the use of the sister's inhaler, and keeps questions short while Wesley is distressed.
History
Characterises the breathing problem:
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 4 are elicited, including the preceding cold.

kids.x: Onset and course: came on over a few hours overnight, bad for 3 hours, constant and worsening
Noise: expiratory wheeze like his sister's asthma; no stridor
Preceding cold for 2 days (runny nose, mild cough), now improving while the breathing worsens
Response to treatment: two puffs of his sister's salbutamol at about 5 am, without a spacer, helped a little

check.x: Asks how unwell he is: tiredness and behaviour (more tired, not himself), ability to talk, colour (no blue lips), eating and drinking (eating less, drinking a little) and urine output (fewer wees).
Asks about previous episodes and interval symptoms: bronchiolitis at 8 months without intensive care, no wheeze since, no night cough or exercise wheeze when well.
Explores triggers and exposures: viral illness from day-care, and household smoking (mother smokes about 10 a day, sometimes indoors).
Asks about features of the dangerous differentials:
check.d: Credit when anaphylaxis and an inhaled foreign body are both asked about, plus at least one of the other two.

kids.x: Anaphylaxis: rash or hives, lip or face swelling, vomiting, floppiness, new foods, bites or stings, previous reactions
Inhaled foreign body: sudden choking or coughing episode, access to small objects
Croup or epiglottitis: barking cough, stridor, hoarse or muffled voice, drooling, tripod position, immunisation status
Pertussis: coughing fits, whoop, vomiting after coughing

check.x: Asks about chronic or congenital causes: cystic fibrosis or protracted bacterial bronchitis (newborn screen normal, no chronic wet cough, growing well) and laryngomalacia (never noisy breathing when well).

Takes a paediatric background history (BINDS): born at 36+4 by vaginal delivery, immunisations up to date, varied diet but eating less now, milestones met and on the 65th centile, poor sleep for 2 nights, day trained with fewer wees.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 of the 5 BINDS domains are covered, including immunisations.

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: eczema since 6 months on emollients and a topical steroid, the sister's salbutamol, and no food or medicine allergies.
Takes a family history of atopy: older sister with asthma, father with eczema.
Takes a social history: parents separated, a week in each home, day-care Monday to Wednesday, who smokes in which home.
Explores Kate's ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders about asthma like his sister or bronchiolitis again, is worried he is getting worse, wants treatment now and to know whether he will stay.
Examination

General inspection: alertness and behaviour (alert, a bit grizzly but settles on his mother's lap), colour (no cyanosis), speech (short sentences), posture, coryza, and the absence of drooling and stridor.
Assesses work of breathing: respiratory rate, tracheal tug, subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, accessory muscle use and head bobbing.
Auscultates the chest and finds widespread bilateral expiratory wheeze with a prolonged expiratory phase, good equal air entry (not a silent chest), and no focal crackles or bronchial breathing.
Assesses perfusion and hydration: heart rate, CRT, mucous membranes, eyes and skin turgor (not clinically dehydrated).
Inspects the skin for urticaria and angioedema (none) and notes the flexural eczema. Examines the throat and ears (mildly red throat, normal ear drums).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR, SpO2, heart rate and moderate respiratory distress in the yellow zone of the 1 to 4 year chart and slightly worse between sets, calling for clinical review by a senior doctor and closer observation. SpO2 is above 92%, so oxygen is not yet needed. Temperature is low-grade and CRT normal.
check.d: Accept the candidate also reporting the response to the first salbutamol dose given in Part 1 (RR 40, SpO2 95%, persisting subcostal recession and wheeze, HR 156).

check.x: Grades the episode as moderate: alert, moderate recession, talking in short sentences, SpO2 93–94% in air. Names the features that would make it severe or life-threatening: agitation or drowsiness, marked work of breathing, unable to talk, silent chest, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92% in air, or poor response to treatment.
check.d: Credit when moderate severity is justified and at least 3 escalation features are named. Accept moderate-to-severe if justified from work of breathing, provided escalation is appropriate.

check.x: Interprets the PCR: rhinovirus/enterovirus detected, all else (including RSV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and pertussis) not detected. This fits a viral trigger, does not change acute management, no antibiotics, because there are no clinical features of bacterial infection (no focal signs, he is not septic), and contact and droplet precautions apply.
check.d: Credit when rhinovirus/enterovirus detected with the rest negative is read correctly and the candidate says it does not change acute management or call for antibiotics. Infection-control precautions are a bonus.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as viral-induced (preschool) wheeze, justified by at least 3 of: acute expiratory wheeze and increased work of breathing after a cold, partial response to salbutamol, a previous wheezy illness, smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth, his own eczema and family atopy.
check.d: Accept acute asthma if the candidate links it to the viral trigger.

check.x: Names at least 3 differentials, each with a feature against it, including anaphylaxis or an inhaled foreign body: bronchiolitis (he is 3), pneumonia (no focal signs), inhaled foreign body (no choking, bilateral symmetrical wheeze), anaphylaxis (no skin signs or exposure), acute asthma.
Management

Prescribes salbutamol 100 microgram/puff by puffer and small-volume spacer with a mask: 6 puffs (RCH: 6 puffs under 6 years) every 20 minutes for 3 doses in the first hour, reassessing after each dose.
Gives oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%, target 92% or above.
If severe or not responding, adds ipratropium 21 microgram/puff, 4 puffs (RCH: 4 puffs age 1–5 years) with each salbutamol dose in the first hour.
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg (15 mg) only if severe, not responding or admitted; not routine for preschool viral-induced wheeze.
check.d: Optional: maximum 40 mg once daily for up to 3 days (Australian Asthma Handbook; Queensland Preschool wheeze), or the RCH regimen of 2 mg/kg (maximum 60 mg) on day 1 then 1 mg/kg (maximum 40 mg).

check.x: No routine chest X-ray, bloods or antibiotics.
check.d: Optional: chest X-ray only if pneumonia or a foreign body is suspected or he does not respond; septic work-up only if sepsis is suspected.

check.x: Plans escalation if he does not respond or develops life-threatening features: paediatric registrar and ICU involvement, IV access, IV magnesium sulfate, IV corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg or hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg 6-hourly), and consideration of IV salbutamol in ICU.
check.d: Credit when the candidate names paediatric registrar/ICU involvement, IV access and IV magnesium sulfate. IV corticosteroid (with or without the dose), IV salbutamol and continuous nebulised salbutamol with oxygen are optional extras.

check.x: Discharges when stable on 3-hourly salbutamol, not needing oxygen and drinking, with a written action plan and his own puffer and spacer; otherwise admits.
check.d: Optional: involves the paediatric registrar, weans salbutamol, arranges GP review in 2–3 days. Also credit 'his own salbutamol and spacer, not his sister's' when the candidate gives it in answer to Kate's question in question 4: he needs his own puffer and spacer so the dose reaches his lungs and his sister keeps hers.

check.x: Addresses smoke exposure without judgement: a smoke-free home and car, and an offer of quit support (Quitline 13 7848, GP for nicotine replacement).
check.d: Bonus, not required: credit when raised in question 3 or 4.

check.x: Teaches spacer technique to Kate:
check.d: Credit when the 4 core steps are given (seal over nose and mouth, one puff at a time, 4 normal breaths, shake before each puff); the why and care sub-items, and checking expiry, priming and attaching, are optional.

kids.x: Optional: why: without a spacer much of the medicine stays in the mouth and throat and does not reach the lungs

Core steps: make a good seal over the nose and mouth; one puff; 4 normal breaths; remove and shake again before each puff; repeat for the prescribed number of puffs. Optional: check the expiry date, prime the puffer, attach it to the spacer with the mask
Optional bonus: care: wash monthly in warm water with detergent, drip dry and never wipe it (static makes the medicine stick to the walls)

check.x: Safety netting

Tells Kate in plain words to call 000 if his lips go blue, he becomes drowsy or floppy, is too breathless to talk or drink, or the puffer is not helping. Tells her to come back to ED if he needs the puffer more often than every 3 hours, is sucking in at the neck or ribs, or is drinking poorly with fewer wees.
Optional bonus: explains that further wheezy episodes, or wheeze between colds, should be reviewed by the GP for asthma.
check.d: Optional bonus; not required. GP review in 2–3 days is credited under item 36.

part2.lead: Here are Wesley's observations and the result of his respiratory viral PCR.
part2.patient:
Ask this one question only after the examiner reads question 4:

  • "Can't we just keep using his sister's puffer?"

If the candidate is kind and does not judge you, you accept their advice. If they lecture you, go quiet. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets were taken on room air, at triage and just before the medical review, before the first ED salbutamol dose. Two puffs of his sister's salbutamol were given at home at about 05:00 without a spacer. Weight 15 kg.
handover.model:
• Read (NSW paediatric chart, 1 to 4 years): at 06:40, RR 44, SpO2 94% on room air, HR 155 and moderate respiratory distress are all in the yellow zone. BP 98/62, temperature 37.8 °C, CRT 2 seconds and alertness are white. At 06:55 RR is 46, SpO2 93% and HR 158: still yellow and slightly worse. Parental concern is recorded.
  • Meaning: a moderate acute wheezy episode with increased work of breathing. The tachycardia mainly reflects respiratory distress; 37.8 °C is a raised temperature below the fever threshold. Perfusion is normal and there is no shock. SpO2 is above 92%, so oxygen is not yet indicated. The trend is the wrong way.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now, with more frequent observations and inhaled salbutamol started. Any red zone value (severe distress, SpO2 below 90%, a change in conscious state) calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: Triage: to paediatric acute bay, SpO2 probe on, weighed 15 kg, nasal swab taken
Repeat set before medical review; before first ED salbutamol dose

handover.label: Respiratory viral PCR
handover.result: Nasopharyngeal swab collected at triage 06:40. Rapid multiplex respiratory PCR, resulted 07:50. Collected for infection control and bed placement.
handover.model:
• Read: rhinovirus/enterovirus detected. SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, RSV, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, adenovirus and Bordetella pertussis not detected.
  • Meaning: rhinovirus is the commonest trigger of preschool wheeze and fits the 2-day cold. RSV is negative, and at 3 years he is outside the age for bronchiolitis. Pertussis is not detected. The result supports the diagnosis but was not needed to make it.
  • Changes: it does not change acute management. No antibiotics, because there are no clinical features of bacterial infection (no focal signs, he is not septic). Contact and droplet precautions. No chest X-ray or bloods unless he has focal signs or does not respond.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Wesley Morgan, including your interpretation of these results.
How severe is Wesley's episode, and what would make it severe or life-threatening? What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Wesley now, here in the emergency department.
Wesley is going home with his own salbutamol puffer and spacer. Teach his mother the key steps of using the spacer, then tell her when to call 000 or come back.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Wesley Morgan, 3 years, 15 kg.
  • Situation: acute wheeze with moderate work of breathing; RR 46, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 158, all yellow zone and slightly worse between sets. Accept the candidate also reporting the response to the first salbutamol dose given in Part 1 (RR 40, SpO2 95%, persisting subcostal recession and wheeze, HR 156).
  • Background: 2-day cold, wheeze over a few hours overnight, worsening for 3 hours; sister's salbutamol helped a little; bronchiolitis at 8 months; eczema; born 36+4; immunised; maternal smoking; family atopy; eating and passing urine less; no allergies.
  • Assessment: moderate viral-induced wheeze; bilateral expiratory wheeze, good air entry, no focal signs, no features of anaphylaxis or foreign body; PCR rhinovirus/enterovirus, all else negative: fits a viral trigger, does not change management, no antibiotics; contact and droplet precautions.
  • Recommendation: salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour started; please review, and advise on prednisolone and disposition.

Severity: moderate (alert, moderate recession, short sentences, SpO2 93–94% in air). Severe or life-threatening if agitated or drowsy, unable to talk, marked work of breathing, silent chest, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92% in air, or poor response to salbutamol.

Viral-induced (preschool) wheeze, moderate: acute expiratory wheeze and recession after a cold, partial response to salbutamol, rhinovirus on PCR; risk factors: smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth, previous wheezy illness, eczema, family atopy.

  • Acute asthma: for: atopy, sister with asthma; against: no interval or multi-trigger symptoms.
  • Bronchiolitis: against: age 3 (bronchiolitis is under 12 months).
  • Pneumonia: against: no focal crackles or bronchial breathing.
  • Inhaled foreign body: for: toddler with access to Lego; against: no choking episode, bilateral symmetrical wheeze, coryzal prodrome.
  • Anaphylaxis: against: no skin or gut features, no exposure, gradual onset.

1. Paediatric acute bay, SpO2 monitoring, kept calm on Mum's lap; senior review (yellow zone).
  2. Salbutamol 100 microgram/puff by spacer and mask, 6 puffs every 20 minutes for 3 doses (RCH: 6 puffs under 6 years), reassessing after each.
  3. Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%, to keep it at 92% or above.
  4. Severe or not responding: add ipratropium 21 microgram/puff, 4 puffs (RCH age-based dose: 4 puffs under 6 years) to each dose in the first hour.
  5. Prednisolone 1 mg/kg (15 mg) only if severe, not responding or admitted; not routine.
  6. No routine X-ray or bloods; no antibiotics.
  7. Not responding or life-threatening: registrar and ICU, IV access, IV magnesium.
  8. Discharge when stable on 3-hourly salbutamol, no oxygen, drinking: action plan, own puffer and spacer; otherwise admit.

• Spacer, 4 core steps: seal the mask over nose and mouth; one puff at a time; 4 normal breaths; shake before each puff.
  • Optional: why a spacer (more medicine reaches the lungs); check expiry, prime, attach to spacer and mask.
  • 000: blue lips, drowsy or floppy, too breathless to talk or drink, puffer not helping.
  • Back to ED: needing the puffer more than every 3 hours, sucking in at the neck or ribs, poor drinking or fewer wees.
  • Answers Kate: he needs his own puffer and spacer so the dose reaches his lungs and his sister keeps hers; sharing without a spacer delivers little medicine (credited under item 36).
  • Optional (bonus): smoke-free home and car; offer Quitline 13 7848 and nicotine replacement through the GP, without judgement.

ddx.for: Acute expiratory wheeze with recession over a few hours after a 2-day cold, a partial response to salbutamol, rhinovirus on PCR, smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth and atopy.
He has eczema, a sister with asthma, a father with eczema and responds partly to salbutamol.
ddx.against: He has no wheeze or night cough between colds and no other triggers, and at 3 years episodic viral wheeze is more likely.

ddx.for: A viral prodrome with rhinovirus detected, and he had bronchiolitis at 8 months.
ddx.against: He is 3 years old, beyond the under-12-month age group for bronchiolitis, and his wheeze responds to salbutamol.

ddx.for: A cold followed by tachypnoea and a low-grade temperature of 37.8 °C.
ddx.against: The chest signs are bilateral wheeze with good equal air entry and no focal crackles or bronchial breathing.

ddx.for: He is a toddler with access to his sister's Lego.
ddx.against: There was no choking episode, the wheeze is bilateral and symmetrical, and it followed a coryzal illness.

ddx.for: An atopic child with acute wheeze and respiratory distress.
ddx.against: No urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or floppiness, no new food or sting, and the onset was gradual after a cold.

guide:
The student playing the patient plays Kate (Wesley's mother) and gives the nurse's lines. Wesley is imagined on her lap. The nurse gives the triage observations at the start. A good candidate asks for salbutamol by spacer early, before finishing the history, and that earns item 3. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for an X-ray, bloods or the swab result in Part 1, say any results will be given in Part 2. After salbutamol his heart rate stays fast; this is expected and he is otherwise improving, so do not mark a candidate down for continuing treatment rather than escalating. In Part 2, hand over both results, then ask the four questions in order. Kate asks her one question after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate treats early, then takes a structured history. They time the wheeze against the cold, ask about the sister's salbutamol and the smoking, and specifically exclude anaphylaxis and an inhaled foreign body. They cover BINDS, eczema and family atopy without losing time. They assess work of breathing and listen for air entry as well as wheeze. In Part 2 they grade the episode as moderate, name what would make it severe, and say the PCR does not change management. They give correct per-kg and age-based doses, know the oxygen threshold of 92%, plan escalation, and teach the spacer step by step with clear safety netting.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history, forgets anaphylaxis or a foreign body, and does not ask about smoke exposure or hydration. They may call it bronchiolitis in a 3-year-old, give oxygen at 93% without reason, order an X-ray and antibiotics routinely, or give vague spacer instructions. No bronchodilator in the face of yellow zone observations, or discharge with no action plan or no inhaler of his own, is a safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: viral-induced (preschool) wheeze

Viral-induced wheeze is a continuous, high-pitched expiratory wheeze with increased work of breathing in a preschool child, usually triggered by a viral respiratory infection. It is very common: up to a third of children have an episode before the age of 3. It is not the same as asthma. Preschool children have small-calibre airways that narrow easily with viral inflammation, and most grow out of episodic viral wheeze. Recurrent or multi-trigger wheeze (with exercise, laughing, allergens or at night between colds) is a risk factor for later asthma. Wesley has the typical story: a cold for 2 days, wheeze and breathlessness coming on over a few hours overnight and worsening, and a partial response to his sister's salbutamol. He also has several risk factors: tobacco smoke at home (a major risk factor), day-care, birth at 36 weeks, a previous wheezy illness (bronchiolitis), his own eczema, and a family history of asthma and eczema.

The history from a parent

  • The wheeze: onset, duration and course, what it sounds like (expiratory wheeze, not inspiratory stridor), the preceding illness, and any treatment given and its effect.
  • How unwell: behaviour and alertness, talking, colour, eating and drinking, and wet nappies or wees.
  • Previous episodes: past wheeze, hospital or ICU admissions, and symptoms between colds.
  • Paediatric background (BINDS): Birth, Immunisations, Nutrition (and growth), Development, Sleep, plus toileting.
  • Medicines, allergies, family atopy and social history, especially smoke exposure and who the child lives with.

Differentials to ask about

  • Anaphylaxis: skin involvement (urticaria, angioedema) with respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological or gut involvement; a new food, a bite or sting; previous reactions. This is the red flag that must be excluded, because it needs intramuscular adrenaline, not salbutamol (RCH: Anaphylaxis).
  • Inhaled foreign body: a sudden choking episode, access to small objects, and one-sided signs.
  • Croup and epiglottitis: barking cough, stridor and hoarse voice; drooling, a muffled voice, tripod positioning and immunisation status.
  • Pertussis: paroxysmal cough, whoop and post-tussive vomiting; immunisation status.
  • Bronchiolitis (infants under 12 months) and pneumonia (fever, focal crackles or bronchial breathing).
  • Chronic causes: cystic fibrosis and protracted bacterial bronchitis (newborn screening, chronic wet cough, failure to thrive), bronchiolitis obliterans, and laryngomalacia (noisy breathing even when well).

Assessing severity

Severity is a clinical judgement. It rests on mental state, work of breathing, ability to talk, auscultation and response to treatment, with SpO2 as a supporting sign. Features of a moderate to severe episode include an irritable or distressed child, tachycardia, tachypnoea, moderate to marked work of breathing with accessory muscle use, marked limitation in talking and SpO2 below 92%. Drowsiness, a silent chest, cyanosis, bradypnoea, exhaustion or hypotension indicate a life-threatening episode. RCH uses SpO2 below 92% in air as the threshold for oxygen and as a marker of a more severe episode. Wesley is alert and settles on his mother's lap, has mild to moderate recession, talks in short sentences and has SpO2 93 to 94% in air, so this is a moderate episode. The trend between his two sets of observations is slightly worse, which calls for prompt treatment and senior review.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR, SpO2, heart rate and moderate respiratory distress are in the yellow zone of the NSW 1 to 4 year chart, so he needs a clinical review and closer observation. Any red zone value calls for a rapid response. Tachycardia is expected with respiratory distress and after salbutamol; 37.8 °C is a raised temperature below the fever threshold.
  • Respiratory viral PCR: rhinovirus is the commonest trigger of preschool wheeze. The result fits the story but was not needed for the diagnosis, and it does not change treatment. It guides infection control. Finding a virus does not by itself exclude bacterial infection; the decision not to give antibiotics rests on the clinical picture (no focal signs, not septic).
  • Investigations are not routinely needed. Chest X-ray is for suspected pneumonia, a foreign body or a poor response to treatment. A septic work-up is only for suspected sepsis.

Management (RCH Acute asthma; Queensland Preschool wheeze)

  1. Salbutamol 100 microgram/puff by pMDI and small-volume spacer with a mask: 6 puffs for a child under 6 years (RCH age-based dose), every 20 minutes for 3 doses in the first hour, reassessing after each dose. A spacer works as well as a nebuliser and has fewer side effects.
  2. Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%.
  3. Ipratropium bromide 21 microgram/puff, 4 puffs for a child under 6 years (RCH age-based dose), added to each salbutamol dose in the first hour for a severe episode or a poor response.
  4. Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (15 mg; maximum 40 mg) once daily for up to 3 days only if the episode is severe, he does not respond to the first hour of salbutamol, or he needs admission. It is not routine for preschool viral-induced wheeze (Australian Asthma Handbook; Queensland Preschool wheeze). The RCH regimen of 2 mg/kg (maximum 60 mg) on day 1 then 1 mg/kg (maximum 40 mg) is also acceptable.
  5. Not responding or life-threatening: senior and ICU involvement, IV access, IV magnesium sulfate (RCH: 50 mg/kg, maximum 2 g, over 20 minutes), IV corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg or hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg 6-hourly), and IV salbutamol in ICU.
  6. Disposition: stretch salbutamol to 3-hourly. Discharge when he is stable on 3-hourly salbutamol, needs no oxygen and is drinking. Admit under paediatrics if he is not. He goes home with a written action plan and his own puffer and spacer.

Spacer teaching

Without a spacer, much of the dose from a puffer lands in the mouth and throat. A young child needs a small-volume spacer with a mask. Check the expiry date, shake and prime the puffer, and attach it to the spacer. Seal the mask over the nose and mouth, fire one puff, and let the child take 4 normal breaths. Remove the puffer, shake it again before the next puff, and repeat for the prescribed number of puffs. Wash the spacer monthly in warm water with detergent and let it drip dry. Do not wipe it, because wiping builds up static and the medicine sticks to the walls.

Safety netting and follow-up

Parents should call 000 for blue lips, drowsiness or floppiness, a child too breathless to talk or drink, or a puffer that is not helping. They should return to ED if the puffer is needed more often than every 3 hours, the child is sucking in at the neck or ribs, or is drinking poorly with fewer wet nappies. GP review within a few days checks recovery, the action plan, inhaler technique and eczema care. Smoke exposure is a modifiable risk factor: offer quit support (Quitline 13 7848, nicotine replacement through the GP) and advise a smoke-free home and car. Recurrent episodes, or wheeze between colds, should prompt review for asthma and for whether a preventer is needed.
points: In a wheezy preschool child, always ask about anaphylaxis (skin signs with another system involved, new foods, stings) and an inhaled foreign body (sudden choking), because both need different, urgent treatment.
Viral-induced wheeze is common under 3 and is not the same as asthma. Recurrent or multi-trigger wheeze, atopy and smoke exposure raise the risk of later asthma.
Grade severity clinically: mental state, work of breathing, ability to talk and air entry. A silent chest, drowsiness, cyanosis or SpO2 below 92% in air means a severe or life-threatening episode.

Salbutamol by spacer and mask (6 puffs under 6 years, every 20 minutes for 3 doses in the first hour) is first-line. Add ipratropium 4 puffs if severe; give oxygen only below 92%. No routine X-ray, bloods or antibiotics.
Discharge only when the child is stable on 3-hourly salbutamol, with a written action plan, the child's own puffer and spacer, and hands-on spacer teaching.
Safety-net in plain words (000 for blue lips, drowsiness or a puffer that is not helping), arrange GP review in a few days, and address household smoking without judgement.
